name: Performance Review
description: Randall is a software engineer at a company with $$$N$$$ employees. Every year, the company re-evaluates its employees. At the end of every year, the company replaces its several worst-performing employees and replaces with the same number of new employees, so that the company keeps having $$$N$$$ employees. Each person has a constant performance and can be represented by an integer (higher integer means better performance), and no two people have the same performance. The performance of the initial employees are represented by an array of integers $$$A = [A_1, A_2, \dots, A_N]$$$ where $$$A_i$$$ is the performance of the $$$i^{th}$$$ employee. Randall is employee $$$1$$$, so his performance is $$$A_1$$$. We will consider the first $$$M$$$ years. At the end of the $$$i^{th}$$$ year, the company replaces its $$$R_i$$$ worst-performing employees and replaces with $$$R_i$$$ new employees. The performance of these new employees are represented by an array of integers $$$B_i = [(B_i)_1, (B_i)_2, \dots, (B_i)_{R_i}]$$$ where $$$(B_i)_j$$$ is the performance of the $$$j^{th}$$$ new employee. He will consider $$$Q$$$ scenarios. On the $$$i^{th}$$$ scenario, he will change the value of $$$(B_{X_i})_{Y_i}$$$ to $$$Z_i$$$. For each scenario, Randall is wondering whether he will still be in the company after $$$M$$$ years. Note that the changes in each scenario are kept for the subsequent scenarios.
input_specification: Input begins with a line containing three integers: $$$N$$$ $$$M$$$ $$$Q$$$ ($$$2 \le N \le 100\,000$$$; $$$1 \le M, Q \le 100\,000$$$) representing the number of employees, the number of years to be considered, and the number of scenarios, respectively. The next line contains $$$N$$$ integers: $$$A_i$$$ ($$$0 \le A_i \le 10^9$$$) representing the performance of the initial employees. The next $$$M$$$ lines each contains several integers: $$$R_i$$$ $$$(B_i)_1$$$, $$$(B_i)_2$$$, $$$\cdots$$$, $$$(B_i)_{R_i}$$$ ($$$1 \le R_i \lt N$$$; $$$0 \le (B_i)_j \le 10^9$$$) representing the number of employees replaced and the performance of the new employees, respectively. It is guaranteed that the sum of $$$R_i$$$ does not exceed $$$10^6$$$. The next $$$Q$$$ lines each contains three integers: $$$X_i$$$ $$$Y_i$$$ $$$Z_i$$$ ($$$1 \le X_i \le M$$$; $$$1 \le Y_i \le R_{(X_i)}$$$; $$$0 \le Z_i \le 10^9$$$) representing a scenario. It is guaranteed that all integers in all $$$A_i$$$, $$$(B_i)_j$$$, and $$$Z_i$$$ (combined together) are distinct.
output_specification: For each scenario in the same order as input, output in a line an integer $$$0$$$ if Randall will not be in the company after $$$M$$$ years, or $$$1$$$ if Randall will still be in the company after $$$M$$$ years.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1252G — Performance Review [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
